fixes.explanation: Paul says, "On the first day of every week, each of you should set aside a portion of his income, saving it up…" (1 Corinthians 16:2). The reason he gives is "…so that when I come no collections will be needed." A little at a time, every week. That's a plan even I could stick to, and I once forgot a whole batch in the oven.

You've got the weekly rhythm, friend, but the text says the first day, not the last. Paul says to set aside a portion on "…the first day of every week…" (1 Corinthians 16:2). The last day of the week is when I'm checking the bottom of the cookie jar and finding crumbs.

Paul says, "…I will send letters with those you recommend to carry your gift to Jerusalem." (1 Corinthians 16:3). So the Corinthians do the recommending, and Paul sends letters along with the ones they recommend. I like that. The Corinthians get a say in who goes.

Soldiers make for a dramatic scene, friend, but the text doesn't mention any. Paul says he will send letters "…with those you recommend…" to carry the gift (1 Corinthians 16:3). The carriers are people the Corinthians recommend.

Paul says the people the Corinthians recommend will "…carry your gift to Jerusalem." (1 Corinthians 16:3). That's the destination for the gift for the saints. Jerusalem, friend, is easy to remember and hard to say with a mouthful of cookie.

Damascus is a real place too, but the text sends this gift somewhere else. Paul says it goes "to Jerusalem" (1 Corinthians 16:3). The carriers are the people the Corinthians recommend, and Jerusalem is where they're going.

The gift does come up in this chapter, but not as the reason for Timothy. Paul says to see that Timothy has nothing to fear, "…for he is doing the work of the Lord, just as I am." (1 Corinthians 16:10). The text doesn't say anything about Timothy carrying the gift. The reason is his work.

That's right. Paul says, "Send him on his way in peace so that he can return to me, for I am expecting him along with the brothers." (1 Corinthians 16:11). He's expecting Timothy back, so the Corinthians are to send him off, not keep him. A good host knows when to wave goodbye.
Paul did strongly urge him, but the text says, "He was not at all inclined to go now…" (1 Corinthians 16:12). So Apollos isn't leaving right away. Paul says he will go when he has the opportunity.

It's not a flat no forever. Paul says Apollos "…was not at all inclined to go now, but he will go when he has the opportunity." (1 Corinthians 16:12). The word that matters is "now." Paul says he will go later, when the opportunity comes.
The text doesn't call them elders. Paul says Stephanas and his household "…were the first converts in Achaia…" (1 Corinthians 16:15). Their serving comes right after in the same verse.
Tested doesn't fit what the verse says. Paul says, "For they refreshed my spirit and yours as well." (1 Corinthians 16:18). Refreshed is the word, and it's a good one.
